title: Are There Civic Returns to Education?
research_question: Does additional educational attainment causally affect adult civic engagement and attitudes, including voter participation, volunteering, group memberships, support for free speech, and civic awareness? Are the strong correlations between schooling and civic outcomes documented in prior literature reflective of true externalities of education, or are they driven by unobserved individual, family, and community traits?
data_description: The study draws on two datasets. The first is the High School and Beyond (HS&B) longitudinal study, following a cohort of 1980 high school sophomores with follow-ups in 1984 (age ~20) and 1992 (age ~28), yielding roughly 11,000-12,000 individual observations with measures of college entrance (attendance at junior, community, or 4-year colleges by 1984) and four 1992 civic outcomes: voter registration, voting in the past year, voting in the 1988 Presidential election, and recent volunteering. HS&B is augmented with school-level data (including miles to nearest 2-year college), county-level counts of 2-year colleges in 1983 from HEGIS, and state/county controls. The second dataset is the pooled 1972-2000 General Social Surveys (GSS), restricted to U.S. residents at age 16 who turned 14 between 1914 and 1978, providing measures of years of schooling, voter turnout in the last Presidential election, newspaper readership frequency, group memberships, and attitudes toward free speech for various groups.
institutional_context: Two distinct settings generate plausibly exogenous variation in schooling. First, the U.S. system of junior and community colleges expanded unevenly across states during the mid-20th century, shaped by state-specific enabling legislation and enrollment pressures from the G.I. Bill, the baby boom, and migration. By the early 1980s, states like California, Texas, Washington, Arizona, Illinois, and Michigan had extensive public 2-year college systems, while others had far fewer institutions. This geographic variation affected the cost of college entrance for teens, particularly those from disadvantaged backgrounds. Second, U.S. states historically set differing minimum schooling and age requirements before youth could obtain work permits and enter the labor force. These compulsory schooling and child-labor regulations varied across states and over time from 1914 to 1978, with stricter laws (requiring 9 or more years of schooling) constraining when teens could leave school for work, thereby influencing secondary educational attainment, especially among children from less-educated families.
